title: Talking about language
subtitle: syntax, lexicon, register, eloquent, mot juste
summary: Use the specialist terms for describing language - syntax, phonology, lexicon, orthography, morphology - and the everyday words for using language well or badly.

lesson.heading: Specialist terms
rows: the grammar and word order of a language
the sound system: pronunciation and intonation
a specialised term for writing systems and spelling

lesson.heading: Modality, phonemes and morphemes
lesson.text: Different languages express **modality** - meanings such as possibility and necessity - in different ways; English does it with modal verbs like must, could and should. All languages have **phonemes**, the different sounds that distinguish meanings, and English has ten **diphthongs**, sounds made by combining vowels. **Morphemes** are units of meaning: unthinkable has three, un, think and able.

examples.text: **Modality** is expressed in different forms in different languages.
Some world languages have very few vowel **phonemes** and no **diphthongs**.
There are three **morphemes** in unthinkable.

lesson.heading: Writing systems
lesson.text: The English alphabet has 26 **characters** - letters or symbols. Some writing systems, such as Chinese, are not alphabetic but have **pictograms**, characters representing pictures, or **ideograms**, characters representing ideas and concepts.

examples.text: The **orthography** of Burmese is quite difficult for a foreign learner.
Japanese uses several different writing systems, with hundreds of **characters**.
This ancient and beautiful alphabet uses **pictograms** to express meaning.
The **lexicon** of a language like English is constantly changing.

lesson.heading: Meanings in context
lesson.text: Many English words are **polysemous** - they have a number of different meanings - and the meaning is usually clear from the **context**, the language or situation around the word. Words are often used in a **metaphorical** way, a way that is not literal: to see the light means to understand something.

examples.text: Many words in English are **polysemous**.
'It's not fair that the boy with the fair hair won all the prizes at the fair' is an example of **polysemy**.
'Life is a journey and sometimes your path will be rocky' is a **metaphor**.

lesson.heading: Usage, register and jargon
lesson.text: Language **usage** - the way words are used - changes with time. Some words become **obsolete**, that is fall out of use, while new words are **coined**, or created. A **register** is the style of language used in a particular situation, formal or informal. **Jargon** is language used by a particular group who share a job or interest.

examples.text: Some words become **obsolete** while new words are **coined**.
Any language has a number of different **registers**.
'What kind of external storage device do you have access to?' is computer **jargon**.
'Marry, thou art roinish, forsooth' is **obsolete** language.

lesson.heading: Using language well
lesson.text: Someone **articulate** can express their ideas clearly in words; someone **eloquent** expresses ideas or opinions clearly in a way that may influence others. To say something in a **succinct** way is to say it clearly and in few words, and the **mot juste** is exactly the right word for the situation.

examples.text: Sam is so good with words - he can always find the **mot juste**.
I love listening to her - she's such an **eloquent** speaker.
We don't have much time, so I'll be as **succinct** as possible.

lesson.note: Mot juste is French for 'correct word'.

lesson.heading: Using language badly
lesson.text: Someone **inarticulate** is unable to express their ideas clearly. If you are **speechless** or **lost for words**, you are so surprised that you cannot say anything. If you **put your foot in it**, you say something without thinking and may upset or embarrass someone.

examples.text: I couldn't understand a word of what he was saying - he was completely **inarticulate**.
I couldn't believe she'd lost all my money - I was completely **speechless**!
I was completely **lost for words** when Adam told me he'd quit his job.
I think I **put my foot in it** when I asked Sara how Tom was. I didn't realise they'd split up!

exercises.prompt: Match each specialist term with what it covers.

pairs.right: the sound system of a language

exercises.prompt: Japanese uses several different writing systems, with hundreds of ___.
exercises.explanation: Characters are the letters or symbols of a writing system.

exercises.prompt: The ___ of a language like English is constantly changing as new words are coined.
exercises.explanation: Lexicon is the specialised term for the vocabulary of a language.

exercises.prompt: This ancient and beautiful alphabet uses ___ to express meaning through pictures.
exercises.explanation: Pictograms represent pictures; ideograms represent ideas or concepts.

exercises.prompt: Sam is so good with words - he can always find the ___.
exercises.explanation: The mot juste is exactly the right word or phrase for a particular situation.

exercises.prompt: I love listening to her - she's such an ___ speaker.
exercises.hint: (able to influence others with clear ideas)
exercises.explanation: An eloquent speaker expresses ideas clearly in a way that may influence others.

exercises.prompt: We don't have much time, so I'll be as ___ as possible.
exercises.explanation: To be succinct is to express something clearly using few words.

exercises.prompt: I think I put my ___ in it when I asked Sara how Tom was. I didn't realise they'd split up!
exercises.explanation: To put your foot in it is to say something without thinking that may upset or embarrass someone.

exercises.prompt: Meanings connected with probability and obligation are expressed differently in different languages. What is the technical term?
exercises.explanation: Modality covers meanings such as possibility and necessity; English expresses it with modal verbs.

exercises.prompt: Some world languages have very few vowel phonemes and no combinations of vowels. What are these combinations called?
exercises.explanation: Diphthongs are sounds made by combining vowels; English has ten of them.

options: language used by a particular group who share a job or interest
an obsolete word that has fallen out of use
a word with several different meanings
a non-literal use of a word
exercises.explanation: Jargon is the specific type of language used by a particular group sharing a job or interest.

exercises.statement: If a word is obsolete, it has just been coined.
exercises.explanation: Obsolete words have fallen out of use; new words are coined, that is created.

exercises.statement: If you are lost for words, you are so surprised that you are unable to say anything.
exercises.explanation: Correct - you can also say you are speechless.

To see the light, meaning to understand something.

A fine day, a parking fine and a fine wine.

You need to back up your files to the cloud.

exercises.answer: A register is the style of language used in a particular situation
exercises.explanation: Formal and informal are two of the registers any language has.
